newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Top Khmer Rouge leaders split over politics.
newsitem.headline: Top Khmer Rouge leaders split over politics.

text.p: Khmer Rouge nominal leader Khieu Samphan accused a senior comrade in his organisation of treason on Wednesday, revealing a split in the Maoist guerrilla movement behind Cambodia's "killing fields".
Khieu Samphan accused defence chief Son Sen and his wife of spying and seeking to destroy the Khmer Rouge's guerrilla army, called the army of Democratic Kampuchea (Cambodia).
"On June 9, 1997, the army of Democratic Kampuchea caught spies Son Sen, also known as Khieu, and (his wife) Yun Yat...," Khieu Samphan announced on clandestine Khmer Rouge radio.

He accused the couple of working on behalf of Cambodia's current co-premier Hun Sen and neighbouring Vietnam to destroy the army and harm a political alliance recently formed by the country's other prime minister, Prince Norodom Ranariddh.

Relations between Hun Sen and Ranariddh, who formed an uneasy coalition after U.N.-sponsored elections in 1993, have grown increasingly bitter over power-sharing disputes and a keen competition to recruit Khmer Rouge rebels to their own sides.

Khieu Samphan, who has consistently expressed his support for Ranariddh and his National United Front political alliance, urged his rebels to fight Hun Sen, who fled to Vietnam after breaking with the Khmer Rouge in the mid-1970s.
Hun Sen returned in late 1978 with the Vietnamese invasion force that eventually overthrew the 1975-1979 Khmer Rouge regime. He later led the Hanoi-backed government that ruled until 1991.
The Khmer Rouge has been waging a low-intensity war against the coalition government since reneging on the 1991 U.N.-sponsored peace pact that led to the 1993 elections.

But since last August thousands of guerrillas, including one of the group's most senior officials Ieng Sary, have defected to the government and fewer than 2,000 fighters are thought to remain in the last rebel stronghold of Anlong Veng in the country's north.
Analysts say Tuesday's broadcast revealed the most dramatic split in the rebel movement since it started to unravel.

David Ashley, a scholar of the Khmer Rouge, told Reuters that rumours that Ranariddh's group was making contacts with Khieu Samphan and his northern zone commander Ta Mok had apparently prompted Hun Sen to start his own politicking.
"The obvious thing Hun Sen would do would be to try to break up the remaining Khmer Rouge," he said.
Ashley said Ranariddh and Hun Sen were apparently capitalising on the historic rivalry between Ta Mok and Son Sen.
